newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish pound slips vs stg as sterling powers ahead.
newsitem.headline: Irish pound slips vs stg as sterling powers ahead.

text.p: The Irish pound hovered above 2.6300 marks but slipped back below 0.9300 sterling in afternoon trade on Friday as the British currency hit 57-month highs against the mark, dealers said.
Both sterling and the dollar were boosted by market hopes that an accord could be reached on the EU stability pact, putting Economic and monetary union (EMU) back on track.
"Markets are convinced this is just a political dance before agreement is reached," said Colin Hunt, economist at Bank of Ireland Group Treasury.
Analysts say that if the uncertainty surrounding EMU is cleared up in coming days, speculators could come back into the market to sell the Irish pound next week.
"If the EMU uncertainty is washed away, it could be sold back below 2.60 marks," Pat O'Sullivan, economist at AIB Group Treasury, said.
By 1500 GMT, the Irish pound was at 0.9255 sterling against 0.9315 this morning and 0.9297 at Thursday's close.
It firmed to 2.6326 marks from 2.6206 last night, supported by short covering and persistent revaluation rumours.
Several analysts dismissed talk of a revaluation this weekend, saying such a move was highly unlikely under the current Irish caretaker administration.
"I think it's just a red herring," said Bank of Ireland's Hunt. "I don't think you are going to have any move until there is a new finance minister in situ."
Some analysts believe that a new government is unlikely to revalue anyway because it would involve a call on how sterling performs over the next 12 months.
It would also upset exporters and farmers and would be an admission that the Irish pound is closely tied to sterling, they say.
But NCB Stockbroker's Dermot O'Brien thinks revaluation could be a likely option for the incoming Fianna Fail/Progressive Democrat government.

"I think it's a real prospect, the reason being, if the central parity stays where it is, if EMU is back on track and that's still the bet, the pound will grind gradually lower. The central bank won't like that, knowing what impact that will have on inflation," he said.
